title: Test-Time Matching: Unlocking Compositional Reasoning in Multimodal Models
one_liner: The paper shows that many multimodal reasoning scores are held down by the evaluation rule itself, then uses test-time self-training to turn hidden matching skill into higher benchmark accuracy.
lead: Compositional reasoning benchmarks ask a model to connect several facts at once: which caption belongs to which image, which description fits a scene after word order changes, or which pair stays consistent across views. Recent papers reported that multimodal models fail badly on these tasks. This paper argues that part of the failure is real, but part comes from the scoring rule. If a benchmark presents a small group of items that must be matched jointly, scoring each pair in isolation throws away information the model already has about the whole group. The authors first replace that rule with a group matching score that checks whether the model can assign the whole set consistently. They then use those induced group assignments as pseudo-labels at test time and retrain the model on the fly. That procedure, called Test-Time Matching, raises the original benchmark score because it converts weak but structured preferences into a sharper decision rule.

problem.h2: Benchmarks can hide real matching ability
paras: Many multimodal reasoning datasets are built from small groups. A benchmark may give two images and two captions, then ask which caption matches which image. The true answer is a permutation: a full assignment of items to items. But common evaluation rules do not score the permutation directly. They score each pair separately, then combine those local decisions into a final accuracy number.

That matters because compositional reasoning often shows up as relative preference rather than absolute certainty. A model may assign caption A a slightly higher score on image 1 than on image 2, and caption B a slightly higher score on image 2 than on image 1. Jointly, that is enough to recover the correct assignment. Separately, each margin may look weak, so the benchmark reports failure. The paper asks two questions. First, how much ability is already present but hidden by pairwise scoring? Second, can the model use its own joint assignments at test time to sharpen itself without any outside labels?

callout.html: Pairwise scoring can underestimate multimodal compositional reasoning because the task is really a structured assignment problem.

panels.title: 1. Small group with coupled choices
panels.caption: The task is to choose a whole matching, not four unrelated yes or no answers.

panels.title: 2. Pairwise metric scores each edge alone
panels.caption: Each image-caption score is read separately, so small but consistent margins can be missed.

panels.title: 3. Group matching recovers the assignment
panels.caption: Selecting the best assignment across the whole group reveals structure that pairwise scoring hid.

panels.title: 4. Use that assignment as a pseudo-label
panels.caption: At test time, the model trains on its own most consistent group decisions.

panels.title: 5. Original benchmark score rises
panels.viz_args: Margins widen on the same task
panels.caption: Self-training makes the local scores more decisive, so the old metric now credits the model.

steps.text: For each group, compute the model's compatibility score for every possible cross-modal pair.
Choose the permutation with the highest total score across the whole group.
Use the chosen matching as a pseudo-label, which means a training target produced by the model itself rather than by a human annotator.

steps.b: Update the model at test time
steps.text: Run a short self-training loop on the current benchmark examples so the preferred assignment gets a larger score gap over the alternatives.
After the update, rescore the same examples under the benchmark's standard rule and measure how much the sharpened margins change accuracy.

paras: The paper changes the decision rule at evaluation time and then uses that decision rule to drive a temporary adaptation step. The model architecture can stay the same. What changes is how the system interprets the scores the model already produces, and how it feeds those structured decisions back into the model.

hidden.name: assignment margin
paras: The key quantity is not any single pair score. It is the margin between the best full assignment and the runner-up assignment. If that margin is positive, the model already contains a consistent preference for one global interpretation of the group. A weak pairwise metric can miss that because it ignores how the scores combine under the one-to-one matching constraint.

Test-Time Matching tries to enlarge this assignment margin. Once the model commits to one structured assignment, the self-training step pushes the scores so that the chosen permutation remains preferred under small perturbations. That matters because the original benchmark often flips from wrong to right when a few borderline pair scores move just enough to respect the same global choice.

heat.caption: Darker cells matter more for whether a structured matching can be recovered and then reinforced.

reads.html: The model may already know which full arrangement fits best, even when no single pair score is extreme.
Compositional skill is partly stored in relative score structure across a group, and the main signal is the gap between the top joint matching and the alternatives.

paras: The method works because group structure turns noisy local scores into a cleaner supervision signal. When the benchmark enforces one-to-one matching, many incorrect pair combinations cannot all be true at once. Solving the assignment problem filters those incompatible choices away and keeps only the globally consistent arrangement.

The test-time update then sharpens the model around that arrangement. It does not inject new knowledge from outside. It reweights the model's own scores so that the preferred matches move farther above the rejected ones, which means small local ambiguities stop flipping the final answer. This is why the method can help even when the initial benchmark metric hid part of the model's competence.

The same idea can transfer beyond explicit group benchmarks because self-training on structured high-confidence decisions can create cleaner local decision boundaries. In plain terms, the model uses agreement across many related candidate pairs to decide which scores deserve reinforcement.

stages.s: Sharper scores and higher benchmark accuracy

math.words: Score each full assignment by summing the model's pair scores, then choose the assignment with the largest total.
math.equation: match* = argmax over permutations pi of sum_i s(image_i, text_pi(i))
symbols: model score for pairing image i with text j
a permutation, which means a one-to-one assignment of texts to images

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: There are two images and two captions.
The model scores image 1 with caption A at 0.56 and with caption B at 0.44.
It scores image 2 with caption A at 0.46 and with caption B at 0.54.
Assignment one gives A to image 1 and B to image 2, for a total of 1.10.
Assignment two gives B to image 1 and A to image 2, for a total of 0.90.
The first assignment wins, so Test-Time Matching treats it as the temporary target and updates the model to widen that 0.20 gap.

math.note: The important step is not the arithmetic itself. It is the one-to-one constraint, because that constraint converts a set of local scores into a structured decision.

charts.title: Pairwise metric only
charts.note: This view reads each pair mostly in isolation, so consistent but low-margin matchings are easy to miss.

charts.title: Group matching plus TTM
charts.note: The assignment solver creates a global target, and self-training strengthens the same preference, which is why the original benchmark score often rises afterward.

items.html: If the best-scoring assignment is already wrong, self-training can push the model further toward that wrong choice because the update trusts the model's own decision.

items.b: The method depends on useful score structure.
items.html: If all pair scores are nearly random, the assignment margin is noise, so the group solver produces unstable targets and the update has little value.

items.b: Test-time adaptation can overfit tiny benchmarks.
items.html: A short update on a narrow test set may inflate results on that set while teaching little that transfers elsewhere, because the model is tuning to the local candidate pool.

Use benchmarks where the task truly has coupled choices, monitor the assignment margin, and limit the update size because small updates can widen clear global preferences without letting uncertain pseudo-labels dominate the model.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small benchmark with groups of two or three images and matching captions. Show the raw pair scores, the best full assignment, and the runner-up assignment. Then run a short test-time update that uses the chosen assignment as a pseudo-label and plot how the score margins change.

The demo should verify three things. First, some examples that fail under pairwise scoring already contain the correct global matching. Second, the self-training step widens the gap between the chosen assignment and its closest alternative. Third, the widened gap flips the original benchmark decision on at least some borderline cases.
demo.closing: A convincing demo shows that the paper is not claiming magical new reasoning at test time. It is showing how structured matching and short self-training expose and amplify competence that the raw metric only partially captured.
